title: Separation of compute and storage for YugabyteDB
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
Separating computing instances and persistence service, also known as disaggregation of compute and storage, gives the impression that the database servers can be stopped without losing the data service. Cloud vendors may market this as "serverless," but in reality, the physical architecture still involves running servers. A database stored on a disk without CPU and RAM to access it would be useless except for data archiving purposes.

Operational databases require data processing within memory structures: buffer pools, work areas, and transaction states. While it might not be evident to the user, "serverless" services, whether NoSQL like DynamoDB or SQL like Aurora Serverless, must use compute resources (CPU and RAM) on storage servers. Their "serverless" nature comes from not requiring pre-allocated fixed capacity for the instances that interact with your application. This setup allows for scaling up and down the SQL database's query processing layer, which manages connections, query parsing, execution plan optimization, and their execution. In the case of distributed SQL databases, this query processing layer can scale out horizontally to multiple instances.

For example, I was reading this in an AWS blog post about TiDB

TiDB’s architecture separates compute from storage, allowing each component to scale independently. This provides the scalability and flexibility needed for a serverless architecture.

In this article, I'll demonstrate the two-layer architecture of Yugabyte's distributed PostgreSQL database and how it is easy to implement separation of concern between the stateless and stateful layers.

YugabyteDB logically separates "compute" and "storage," as cloud vendors name them in their marketing messages, in its two-layer architecture:

  • The query processing layer, known as YSQL for the PostgreSQL API or YCQL for the Cassandra-like API, manages the application connections and processes queries to execute read/write operations on the storage layer. It is stateless and can scale to provide the same service on multiple nodes. It uses CPU and RAM with limited local storage for temporary tables or work areas that do not fit in memory.
  • The storage and transaction layer, called DocDB, executes these read/write operations and distributes them across its nodes, where data and transaction intents are stored and replicated. It is stateful, but being sharded to small "tablets," it can scale with automatic re-sharding. It accesses persistent storage, like block storage mounted as a local filesystem, and also uses CPU and RAM to optimize the data access (SST files block-based cache, LSM-Tree MemTable) but also offloaded filtering and aggregation (pushdowns).

The default configuration deploys both logical layers on all nodes to optimize resource usage for mixed workloads. All nodes are equal so you can connect to any of them, and data is distributed across all. If you need to physically separate the two layers into different containers or compute instances, it's easy to do so by enabling only the query layer or the storage layer. Here is how to proceed:

  • The nodes dedicated to storage will have their YSQL layer disabled by a simple parameter: enable_ysql=false and will run tablet peers according to the data placement configuration
  • The nodes dedicated to compute will be out of the data placement configuration defined at the cluster level or tablespace level and can optionally be blacklisted from the tablet load balancer

In the following architecture diagram, this means that on each node we can enable or disable the blue and orange layers independently, and I'll demonstrate how to do it.

An example in a Docker lab

I create a network and start one storage node in zone "us1a" 

docker network create yb

docker run -d --name dbus1a01 --hostname dbus1a01 --network yb -p 7000:7000 yugabytedb/yugabyte yugabyted start --background=false --cloud_location=db.us1.us1a --tserver_flags=enable_ysql=false

I create two additional storage nodes in zones "us1b" and "us1c" 

docker run -d --name dbus1b01 --hostname dbus1b01 --network yb yugabytedb/yugabyte yugabyted start --join dbus1a01  --background=false --cloud_location=db.us1.us1b --tserver_flags=enable_ysql=false

docker run -d --name dbus1c01 --hostname dbus1c01 --network yb yugabytedb/yugabyte yugabyted start --join dbus1a01  --background=false --cloud_location=db.us1.us1c --tserver_flags=enable_ysql=false

I can not connect to those nodes because I disabled the SQL query layer, but they can store data (the tablets for table rows, index entries, and transaction intents). By default, data is distributed to all nodes, but before adding the compute nodes, I will restrict data placement. I used "db" as the cloud tag, with one "us" region and three availability zones. 

docker exec dbus1a01 yugabyted configure data_placement --constraint_value=db.us1.us1a,db.us1.us1b,db.us1.us1c

With this configuration, data can be stored in those nodes and re-balanced when additional nodes are added in those availability zones. The cluster is resilient to a single-zone failure. Before creating tables and inserting data, I need at least one compute node.

Let's add two compute nodes in each availability zone: 

for z in us1{a,b,c}
do
 for n in 0{1..2}
 do
  docker run -d --name pg$z$n --hostname pg$z$n --network yb yugabytedb/yugabyte yugabyted start --join dbus1a01  --background=false --cloud_location=pg.us1.$z
 done
done

YSQL is enabled by default, and the only thing I do to make it a compute-only node is change the cloud location to one not part of the data placement. I used "pg" cloud tag for the compute nodes instead of "db" used by the storage node. This is my convention in this example. YugabyteDB pre-defines cloud/region/zone tags that you can use as you want to map to your topology.

I initialize PgBench tables: 

docker run --rm --network yb postgres pgbench -iIdtpfG -h pgus1a01 -p 5433 -U yugabyte yugabyte

On port 7000 (the yb-master web console I exposed from the first node), I can check that only three nodes contain data (tablet peers). The others are stateless with zero tablet peers:

I run PgBench with ten connections distributed to the two compute nodes in zone us1a: 

docker run --rm --network yb -e PGLOADBALANCEHOSTS="random" postgres pgbench -c 10 -T3600 -nN -h pgus1a01,pgus1a02 -p 5433 -U yugabyte yugabyte

Looking at the docker host, I can see the ten connections with their PostgreSQL backend on two docker Cgroups - those of the compute servers:

The tablet servers in the three storage nodes utilize CPU and RAM. This is expected as they handle the processing of reads and writes to the storage. Memory usage includes LSM Tree MemTable, SST Files block cache, and Linux filesystem buffers. Although cloud vendors do not expose this information, it is likely the same in their storage servers, and they hide it by charging storage I/O rather than the CPU and RAM it covers. A database cannot distribute complex queries without offloading filtering and aggregation by pushing down their compute to the storage.

The configuration above, using placement tags, is sufficient to be sure that there are no data in the compute node, but you can add another guarantee by blacklisting each node: 

for z in us1{a,b,c}
do
 for n in 0{1..2}
 do
  docker exec pg$z$n bash -c 'yb-admin --master_addresses=dbus1a01:7100,dbus1b01:7100,dbus1c01:7100 change_blacklist ADD $(hostname -i):9100'
 done
done

Blacklisting is commonly used to scale down, moving out all tablets to other nodes before stopping the node gracefully. It can be used to guarantee that the compute nodes can be scaled down immediately. This also makes it easier to distinguish the compute nodes (blacklisted, with no tablets) from the storage nodes (with data, reads and writes) :

The compute nodes (with no tablets) can scale quickly as they are stateless. The storage nodes can scale but involve data movement to re-balance.

It's worth noting that while it's possible to allocate nodes for SQL query processing (referred to as "compute") and data read/write processing (referred to as "storage") separately to scale them independently, it's not necessarily recommended. I explained this to debunk some myths, such as the misconception that LinkedIn rejected YugabyteDB due to a lack of separation between stateful and stateless layers, as stated in this slide presented by LinkedIn at the PingCAP HTAP summit:

One statement in the slide was incorrect. It is important to note that it is pretty simple to achieve a clean separation between stateful and stateless layers in YugabyteDB. Each YugabyteDB node can run the YSQL query layer, a customized version of PostgreSQL designed to read and write from distributed storage. You have the option of enabling it on the server, exposing its endpoint to the network, or addressing it in the client driver. Additionally, any YugabyteDB can store table, index, and transaction data with complete control over the placement of subsets of the cluster.

It's important to understand that categorizing layers as "compute" and "storage" is mainly for marketing purposes related to "serverless" technologies. If you have access to their resource usage metrics, you might be surprised to find that, in many cases, database services use more compute resources (CPU and RAM) in the "storage" than in the "compute". If this is not the case, it could indicate poor performance, suggesting that the system may not filter and aggregate data efficiently on the "storage" layer before sending it in full to the "compute" layer. This optimization is called "offloading," "smart scan," or "push-downs" and is a must to scale OLTP or Analytics. In YugabyteDB you will see "Storage Filter" and "Partial Aggreggate" in the execution plan's scan nodes.
